RESPONSE.md:3:These are the three assumptions in `PLAN.md` §2 that, if wrong, are most likely to
RESPONSE.md:4:invalidate the design rather than merely delay it. Each is listed with what breaks,
RESPONSE.md:5:what in the plan would change, and how to close it before implementation starts.
RESPONSE.md:7:---
RESPONSE.md:9:## 1. The 24-hour purge and the audit history can be satisfied simultaneously (A9 + A10)
RESPONSE.md:11:**The assumption.** "Accepted" is a server-side status transition, the 24-hour clock
RESPONSE.md:12:starts at the server's acceptance timestamp, and the regulatory audit history can be
RESPONSE.md:13:retained after local customer PII is removed — because the retained audit entries can be
RESPONSE.md:14:pseudonymous (hashes and opaque refs instead of names and addresses).
RESPONSE.md:16:**Why it is the riskiest.** The brief states two requirements that pull in opposite
RESPONSE.md:17:directions: keep an audit history, and delete customer data within 24 hours. If the
RESPONSE.md:18:audit history is legally required to record *who signed* and *what was recorded*, then
RESPONSE.md:19:the very fields that make the audit meaningful are the fields we must delete. There is no
RESPONSE.md:20:engineering trick that resolves this — it is a compliance interpretation, and guessing it
RESPONSE.md:21:wrong produces a regulatory breach that is discovered long after release, on a device
RESPONSE.md:22:that is already in a basement. The secondary risk is the clock: if we key the 24 hours
RESPONSE.md:23:off device time (A13), a skewed clock silently breaches it.
RESPONSE.md:25:**What changes if it is wrong.** If identity must be retained locally, the local purge
RESPONSE.md:26:becomes a partial redaction with a compliance-approved retention carve-out, and the
RESPONSE.md:27:device must be treated as in-scope for longer. If instead the purge is absolute, the
RESPONSE.md:28:audit history must be **server-side only**, and the local audit log can retain nothing
RESPONSE.md:29:but hashes and ids (which is what the plan currently assumes). Either way §8.3 and the
RESPONSE.md:30:`audit_log` / `signatures` tables change, and M4's acceptance criteria change with them.
RESPONSE.md:32:**How to close it.** Written confirmation from compliance on (a) the start of the clock,
RESPONSE.md:33:(b) the exact enumerated field list that counts as "customer data", and (c) whether the
RESPONSE.md:34:audit entry may reference the signer by hash. Then encoded as a test fixture in M0 — not
RESPONSE.md:35:as a comment in the code.
RESPONSE.md:37:---
RESPONSE.md:39:## 2. Field-level conflict resolution is safe with per-record integer versions (A7 + A8)
RESPONSE.md:41:**The assumption.** The backend team can add a small number of additive sync endpoints —
RESPONSE.md:42:notably a change-log/field-level history — and record versions are bumped on *every*
RESPONSE.md:43:write path, including web supervisor edits.
RESPONSE.md:45:**Why it is risky.** The brief says versions are integers on the record. That tells us
RESPONSE.md:46:*that* an inspection changed, never *which field*. Without field-level history, the only
RESPONSE.md:47:available conflict policy is whole-record last-write-wins — which, in an app whose entire
RESPONSE.md:48:purpose is to stop losing inspectors' notes, means the app will systematically discard
RESPONSE.md:49:either the inspector's field notes or the supervisor's correction. That is not a
RESPONSE.md:50:performance problem, it is the original bug reintroduced under a different name. The
RESPONSE.md:51:quieter failure is worse: if even one server write path forgets to bump the version, a
RESPONSE.md:52:client push is accepted as uncontended and overwrites data with **no conflict, no
RESPONSE.md:53:signal, no trace**.
RESPONSE.md:55:**What changes if it is wrong.** If new endpoints are refused, the plan degrades to
RESPONSE.md:56:whole-record LWW with `If-Match`, conflict resolution UI is reduced to "discard and
RESPONSE.md:57:redo", and D3's recommendation must be escalated to inspection-level check-out as a
RESPONSE.md:58:**hard requirement** rather than a follow-on. Data loss becomes an expected, documented
RESPONSE.md:59:product trade-off instead of an incident. If versions are reliable but field history is
RESPONSE.md:60:not, we keep the per-op idempotent push but resolve conflicts by full-record comparison
RESPONSE.md:61:and human review on every divergence.
RESPONSE.md:63:**How to close it.** Written agreement from backend owners in M0 that the three
RESPONSE.md:64:endpoints in §5.1 are in scope, plus an audit of every server write path for version
RESPONSE.md:65:increments, plus a recurring canary job that flags any record whose version fails to
RESPONSE.md:66:advance while `updated_at` does.
RESPONSE.md:68:---
RESPONSE.md:70:## 3. 40 photos per inspection can actually be stored and uploaded in the field (A5 + A6)
RESPONSE.md:72:**The assumption.** Worst-case capture is on the order of a few hundred MB per
RESPONSE.md:73:inspection before optimisation, the device has that headroom, and the connection that
RESPONSE.md:74:returns is slow but usable enough to finish the upload.
RESPONSE.md:76:**Why it is risky.** This is the assumption that fails *in production* rather than in
RESPONSE.md:77:review. It combines three unknowns we have not measured: real file sizes on the oldest
RESPONSE.md:78:tablet in the fleet, free storage after weeks of accumulated inspections, and actual
RESPONSE.md:79:throughput at a job site. The failure mode is insidious: the form data is the part we
RESPONSE.md:80:can protect deterministically, but if an inspector finishes an inspection, drives out of
RESPONSE.md:81:the basement, and the 40 photos never finish uploading, **from their point of view the
RESPONSE.md:82:inspection is still broken** — and they will go back to paper. It also interacts with
RESPONSE.md:83:compliance: photos are customer data and are in scope for the purge, so storage pressure
RESPONSE.md:84:and purge deadlines are competing forces on the same disk.
RESPONSE.md:86:**What changes if it is wrong.** If capture volume is larger or storage tighter than
RESPONSE.md:87:assumed, we must reduce resolution at capture, evict uploaded photos
RESPONSE.md:88:aggressively, and make the pre-offline storage projection blocking (§7.9). If upload
RESPONSE.md:89:throughput is worse, chunk sizing, bounded parallelism, and the "optimised by default"
RESPONSE.md:90:policy (D8) all move from optimisation to requirement — and depot-Wi-Fi upload becomes
RESPONSE.md:91:the expected path rather than the fallback. If the legal requirement is original
RESPONSE.md:92:resolution, the entire storage and upload budget must be re-planned, which is exactly
RESPONSE.md:93:why D8 must be answered before M1 rather than discovered at M3.
RESPONSE.md:95:**How to close it.** Measure all three numbers in M0: actual captured file size on
RESPONSE.md:96:target hardware, free storage across a sample of in-service devices, and throughput from
RESPONSE.md:97:three representative sites. Then set the chunk size, parallelism, and default quality
RESPONSE.md:98:policy from those measurements — and keep `free_storage_bytes`,
RESPONSE.md:99:`local_db_size_bytes`, `attachment_upload_success_rate` and
RESPONSE.md:100:`upload_duration_p95` on the pilot dashboard so the assumptions stay falsifiable after
RESPONSE.md:101:launch.
RESPONSE.md:103:---
RESPONSE.md:105:## Common thread
RESPONSE.md:107:All three share one property: **they cannot be closed by writing better code.** They are
RESPONSE.md:108:a compliance ruling, a cross-team API commitment, and three field measurements. That is
RESPONSE.md:109:why M0's acceptance criteria are stated as evidence and named owners rather than as
RESPONSE.md:110:completed tasks — the rest of the milestone sequence is only as sound as these three
RESPONSE.md:111:answers.

PLAN.md:584:## 13. Rollback
PLAN.md:586:The rollback risk is asymmetric: **turning the feature off eagerly can destroy pending
PLAN.md:587:work.** Therefore rollback is two-phased.
PLAN.md:589:1. **Phase A — Drain mode (always run first).** Flag flips to `drain`: the app stops
PLAN.md:590:   *accepting new* offline edits, pushes everything in the outbox, confirms, and only
PLAN.md:591:   then reverts to online-only. No pending data is ever discarded by a rollback.
PLAN.md:592:2. **Phase B — Hard disable.** Online-only read-through-cache behavior, identical to
PLAN.md:593:   today's app. Used only after the outbox is empty, or in an emergency where retaining
PLAN.md:594:   data is judged less important than stopping harm.
PLAN.md:596:**Rollback triggers** (examples; final list agreed before Stage 1):
PLAN.md:597:- Any confirmed loss of acknowledged input.
PLAN.md:598:- Any purge breach past 24 hours.
PLAN.md:599:- Sync success rate below threshold for a sustained period.
PLAN.md:600:- Crash-free-session regression attributable to the offline stack.
PLAN.md:601:- Data-integrity errors (version mismatches, audit-log gaps) above rate zero.
PLAN.md:603:**Notes:**
PLAN.md:604:- Server-side additions are **additive and independently deployable**, so server
PLAN.md:605:  rollback does not require client rollback; old clients simply never call the new
PLAN.md:606:  endpoints.
PLAN.md:607:- Client rollback is complicated by §9.1: once the store is authoritative, force-killing
PLAN.md:608:  the app to an older build must not wipe a non-empty outbox. Blocks are enforced in the
PLAN.md:609:  migration path.
PLAN.md:610:- **Rollback does not un-retire data.** If a purge already ran, it cannot be undone;
PLAN.md:611:  this is why the purge job is gated behind stage-2 verification rather than enabled at
PLAN.md:612:  stage 0.

PLAN.md:685:| Risk | Why it matters | Mitigation |
PLAN.md:686:|---|---|---|

PLAN.md:689:| Photo volume overwhelms slow links | Inspection never finishes syncing; inspectors lose trust | Optimised derivatives, resumable chunks, bounded parallelism, per-item status, tune from telemetry |
PLAN.md:690:| Version increments missed on some server write path | Client overwrites supervisor edits silently | Audit counters on every write path; canary job comparing version to `updated_at` |
PLAN.md:691:| Conflict rate higher than assumed | Tray becomes daily overhead; product asks for a merge editor | Per-field conflict metrics from day one; fallback is field check-out/locking, not a merge algorithm (D3) |

PLAN.md:696:## 16. Decisions required before implementation (with recommendations)
PLAN.md:698:These must be answered in **M0**; each one changes code, not just wording.
PLAN.md:700:**D1 — Can we add sync-specific endpoints to the server API?**
PLAN.md:701:Recommendation: **yes, add three additive endpoints** (§5.1). Integer per-record
PLAN.md:702:versions alone cannot support field-level merge or an efficient delta pull; without new
PLAN.md:703:endpoints we are forced into last-write-wins on whole records, which *will* discard
PLAN.md:704:supervisor or inspector work. Keeping them additive means zero migration risk for
PLAN.md:705:existing clients.
PLAN.md:706:*If refused:* fall back to whole-record LWW with `If-Match: version`, and accept that
PLAN.md:707:concurrent edits lose data — this should be a written, signed-off product decision.
PLAN.md:709:**D2 — How do we handle form template changes while a tablet is offline?**
PLAN.md:710:Recommendation: **pin `template_version` on the inspection at sync time**; the tablet
PLAN.md:711:renders the pinned schema. On reconnect, if the template changed, treat it as a
PLAN.md:712:**non-blocking** review item for additive/compatible changes and a **blocking** item when
PLAN.md:713:a field the inspector answered was removed or retyped. Never silently re-map answers to
PLAN.md:714:a schema they were not captured against.
PLAN.md:716:**D3 — What happens when supervisor and inspector edit the same field?**

PLAN.md:718:(§6.2). Specifically: inspector wins pre-acceptance, supervisor wins post-acceptance,
PLAN.md:719:and ambiguous divergences go to a human. If the conflict rate turns out to be high, the
PLAN.md:720:next investment should be **whole-inspection check-out** (a soft lock while an inspector
PLAN.md:721:is offline), not a merge algorithm — this matches "no full collaborative editor".
PLAN.md:723:**D4 — How long should the server retain idempotency keys?**
PLAN.md:724:Recommendation: **30 days**, with the practical requirement that it exceeds the maximum
PLAN.md:725:credible offline window plus retry tail (A2). Enforce it as a monitored invariant: alert
PLAN.md:726:if any incoming `op_id` is older than the retention window.
PLAN.md:728:**D5 — How long may a tablet stay offline before re-authentication is required?**

PLAN.md:731:compliance, not from this plan. Do not ship with an unbounded offline window on a device

PLAN.md:734:**D6 — When should photo upload run?**

PLAN.md:736:explicit user override ("upload now"). Also offer "upload on Wi-Fi only" for inspectors

PLAN.md:739:not on network type, by default.
PLAN.md:741:**D7 — Cross-device continuation: in or out?**

PLAN.md:743:local state across devices, which is a materially harder problem. Handle the practical
PLAN.md:744:case operationally for the pilot: an inspection started on the wrong tablet gets
PLAN.md:745:reassigned by a supervisor.
PLAN.md:747:**D8 — Do we upload originals or optimised derivatives?**

PLAN.md:749:purge, configurable per policy.** Evidence first: measure actual file sizes (A5) and the
PLAN.md:750:evidentiary requirement for photos before locking this in — if originals are legally
PLAN.md:751:required, the storage plan (§7.9) and the upload budget change substantially.
PLAN.md:753:**D9 — What encryption do we use for the local database?**
PLAN.md:754:Recommendation: **SQLCipher (or equivalent page-level encryption) with the key in the
PLAN.md:755:platform keystore.** Accept the stated limit (§8.2) and do not market it as stronger
PLAN.md:756:than it is. Verify it against the fleet's oldest hardware for performance impact before
PLAN.md:757:committing.
PLAN.md:759:**D10 — Who owns the "accepted" timestamp, and what exactly counts as customer data?**
PLAN.md:760:Recommendation: **the server owns `accepted_at`**, and the purge scope is fixed as an
PLAN.md:761:explicit, enumerated field list in code (§4 tables) rather than a vague table-wide
PLAN.md:762:delete. Get the enumerated list reviewed by compliance at M0 and turn it into a test
PLAN.md:763:fixture. This is the cheapest place to prevent a regulatory breach.

PLAN.md:767:## 17. Summary of what is deliberately not being built
PLAN.md:769:Automatic text merging; real-time co-editing; peer-to-peer sync; offline reassignment;
PLAN.md:770:cross-device continuation; full-record rewrite of the REST API. Each is a plausible
PLAN.md:771:follow-on once the pilot produces conflict-rate and volume data — none is needed to
PLAN.md:772:solve the problem in `BRIEF.md`.
RESPONSE.md:1:# RESPONSE — The three riskiest assumptions
RESPONSE.md:3:These are the three assumptions in `PLAN.md` §2 that, if wrong, are most likely to
RESPONSE.md:4:invalidate the design rather than merely delay it. Each is listed with what breaks,
RESPONSE.md:5:what in the plan would change, and how to close it before implementation starts.
RESPONSE.md:7:---
RESPONSE.md:9:## 1. The 24-hour purge and the audit history can be satisfied simultaneously (A9 + A10)
RESPONSE.md:11:**The assumption.** "Accepted" is a server-side status transition, the 24-hour clock
RESPONSE.md:12:starts at the server's acceptance timestamp, and the regulatory audit history can be
RESPONSE.md:13:retained after local customer PII is removed — because the retained audit entries can be
RESPONSE.md:14:pseudonymous (hashes and opaque refs instead of names and addresses).
RESPONSE.md:16:**Why it is the riskiest.** The brief states two requirements that pull in opposite
RESPONSE.md:17:directions: keep an audit history, and delete customer data within 24 hours. If the
RESPONSE.md:18:audit history is legally required to record *who signed* and *what was recorded*, then
RESPONSE.md:19:the very fields that make the audit meaningful are the fields we must delete. There is no
RESPONSE.md:20:engineering trick that resolves this — it is a compliance interpretation, and guessing it
RESPONSE.md:21:wrong produces a regulatory breach that is discovered long after release, on a device
RESPONSE.md:22:that is already in a basement. The secondary risk is the clock: if we key the 24 hours
RESPONSE.md:23:off device time (A13), a skewed clock silently breaches it.
RESPONSE.md:25:**What changes if it is wrong.** If identity must be retained locally, the local purge
RESPONSE.md:26:becomes a partial redaction with a compliance-approved retention carve-out, and the
RESPONSE.md:27:device must be treated as in-scope for longer. If instead the purge is absolute, the
RESPONSE.md:28:audit history must be **server-side only**, and the local audit log can retain nothing
RESPONSE.md:29:but hashes and ids (which is what the plan currently assumes). Either way §8.3 and the
RESPONSE.md:30:`audit_log` / `signatures` tables change, and M4's acceptance criteria change with them.
RESPONSE.md:32:**How to close it.** Written confirmation from compliance on (a) the start of the clock,
RESPONSE.md:33:(b) the exact enumerated field list that counts as "customer data", and (c) whether the
RESPONSE.md:34:audit entry may reference the signer by hash. Then encoded as a test fixture in M0 — not
RESPONSE.md:35:as a comment in the code.
RESPONSE.md:37:---
RESPONSE.md:39:## 2. Field-level conflict resolution is safe with per-record integer versions (A7 + A8)
RESPONSE.md:41:**The assumption.** The backend team can add a small number of additive sync endpoints —
RESPONSE.md:42:notably a change-log/field-level history — and record versions are bumped on *every*
RESPONSE.md:43:write path, including web supervisor edits.
RESPONSE.md:45:**Why it is risky.** The brief says versions are integers on the record. That tells us
RESPONSE.md:46:*that* an inspection changed, never *which field*. Without field-level history, the only
RESPONSE.md:47:available conflict policy is whole-record last-write-wins — which, in an app whose entire
RESPONSE.md:48:purpose is to stop losing inspectors' notes, means the app will systematically discard
RESPONSE.md:49:either the inspector's field notes or the supervisor's correction. That is not a
RESPONSE.md:50:performance problem, it is the original bug reintroduced under a different name. The
RESPONSE.md:51:quieter failure is worse: if even one server write path forgets to bump the version, a
RESPONSE.md:52:client push is accepted as uncontended and overwrites data with **no conflict, no
RESPONSE.md:53:signal, no trace**.
RESPONSE.md:55:**What changes if it is wrong.** If new endpoints are refused, the plan degrades to
RESPONSE.md:56:whole-record LWW with `If-Match`, conflict resolution UI is reduced to "discard and
RESPONSE.md:57:redo", and D3's recommendation must be escalated to inspection-level check-out as a
RESPONSE.md:58:**hard requirement** rather than a follow-on. Data loss becomes an expected, documented
RESPONSE.md:59:product trade-off instead of an incident. If versions are reliable but field history is
RESPONSE.md:60:not, we keep the per-op idempotent push but resolve conflicts by full-record comparison
RESPONSE.md:61:and human review on every divergence.
RESPONSE.md:63:**How to close it.** Written agreement from backend owners in M0 that the three
RESPONSE.md:64:endpoints in §5.1 are in scope, plus an audit of every server write path for version
RESPONSE.md:65:increments, plus a recurring canary job that flags any record whose version fails to
RESPONSE.md:66:advance while `updated_at` does.
RESPONSE.md:68:---
RESPONSE.md:70:## 3. 40 photos per inspection can actually be stored and uploaded in the field (A5 + A6)
RESPONSE.md:72:**The assumption.** Worst-case capture is on the order of a few hundred MB per
RESPONSE.md:73:inspection before optimisation, the device has that headroom, and the connection that
RESPONSE.md:74:returns is slow but usable enough to finish the upload.
RESPONSE.md:76:**Why it is risky.** This is the assumption that fails *in production* rather than in
RESPONSE.md:77:review. It combines three unknowns we have not measured: real file sizes on the oldest
RESPONSE.md:78:tablet in the fleet, free storage after weeks of accumulated inspections, and actual
RESPONSE.md:79:throughput at a job site. The failure mode is insidious: the form data is the part we
RESPONSE.md:80:can protect deterministically, but if an inspector finishes an inspection, drives out of
RESPONSE.md:81:the basement, and the 40 photos never finish uploading, **from their point of view the
RESPONSE.md:82:inspection is still broken** — and they will go back to paper. It also interacts with
RESPONSE.md:83:compliance: photos are customer data and are in scope for the purge, so storage pressure
RESPONSE.md:84:and purge deadlines are competing forces on the same disk.
RESPONSE.md:86:**What changes if it is wrong.** If capture volume is larger or storage tighter than
RESPONSE.md:87:assumed, we must reduce resolution at capture, evict uploaded photos
RESPONSE.md:88:aggressively, and make the pre-offline storage projection blocking (§7.9). If upload
RESPONSE.md:89:throughput is worse, chunk sizing, bounded parallelism, and the "optimised by default"
RESPONSE.md:90:policy (D8) all move from optimisation to requirement — and depot-Wi-Fi upload becomes
RESPONSE.md:91:the expected path rather than the fallback. If the legal requirement is original
RESPONSE.md:92:resolution, the entire storage and upload budget must be re-planned, which is exactly
RESPONSE.md:93:why D8 must be answered before M1 rather than discovered at M3.
RESPONSE.md:95:**How to close it.** Measure all three numbers in M0: actual captured file size on
RESPONSE.md:96:target hardware, free storage across a sample of in-service devices, and throughput from
RESPONSE.md:97:three representative sites. Then set the chunk size, parallelism, and default quality
RESPONSE.md:98:policy from those measurements — and keep `free_storage_bytes`,
RESPONSE.md:99:`local_db_size_bytes`, `attachment_upload_success_rate` and
RESPONSE.md:100:`upload_duration_p95` on the pilot dashboard so the assumptions stay falsifiable after
RESPONSE.md:101:launch.
RESPONSE.md:103:---
RESPONSE.md:105:## Common thread
RESPONSE.md:107:All three share one property: **they cannot be closed by writing better code.** They are
RESPONSE.md:108:a compliance ruling, a cross-team API commitment, and three field measurements. That is
RESPONSE.md:109:why M0's acceptance criteria are stated as evidence and named owners rather than as
RESPONSE.md:110:completed tasks — the rest of the milestone sequence is only as sound as these three
RESPONSE.md:111:answers.
